Where it began

Ajit Agarkar was born in Mumbai on 4 December 1977. He started out as a batsman, and his father placed him with the famous coach Ramakant Achrekar, who had him move schools to Shardashram Vidyamandir. He practised at Shivaji Park and made a triple hundred in the Giles Shield at 15.

As a boy he looked up to fast bowlers, Kapil Dev, Michael Holding and Ian Botham among them. When he was told he would have a better chance of a Mumbai place as an all-rounder, he put more into his bowling, and it took him all the way.

The player

He played 26 Tests for India between 1998 and 2006, taking 58 wickets with a best of six for 41, and scoring 571 runs. His finest day with the ball came at the Adelaide Oval in 2003, when that six for 41 helped India to their first Test win in Australia for more than 20 years.

One-day cricket suited him best. Early on he took his first 50 wickets in only 23 matches, a world record at the time, and he was in the India squads that took the Champions Trophy in 2002 and the T20 World Cup in 2007.

What made him special

He had pace and a happy habit of taking wickets just when India needed them. He could hit the ball too: at Lord's in 2002, batting at number eight, he made 109 not out, something plenty of specialist batsmen never managed. In one-day cricket he once made a fifty off 21 balls against Zimbabwe in 2000, an Indian record.

Australia's bowlers did get the better of him for a spell. Seven innings in a row against them brought no runs at all, and the nickname Bombay Duck. That makes the Lord's hundred all the sweeter.

Away from the middle

He played IPL cricket for the Kolkata Knight Riders and the Delhi Daredevils, and in 2013 he captained Mumbai to their 40th Ranji Trophy title, making 145 in the semi-final. He retired later that year and became a cricket analyst and commentator.

He went on to chair India's selection committee until October 2026. In that time India won the T20 World Cup in 2024 and 2026 and the Champions Trophy in 2025.

And finally

He began as a schoolboy batsman tipped to follow Tendulkar, became a fast bowler, and made his Test hundred at the home of cricket anyway. Some talents simply refuse to stay in one box.
